claims.text: Red flag findings: pulse oximetry and chest X-ray; most chronic cough also needs a chest X-ray.
claims.quote: Children with red flag findings should have pulse oximetry and chest radiograph. Most children with chronic cough require a chest radiograph.

claims.text: Suspected foreign body: inspiratory and expiratory chest X-rays, or chest CT in some centers.
claims.quote: If foreign body aspiration is suspected, chest radiograph with inspiratory and expiratory views should be done (or in some centers a chest CT).

claims.text: TB risk or weight loss: chest X-ray plus a PPD skin test or interferon-gamma release assay.
claims.quote: Children with TB risk factors or weight loss should have a chest radiograph and a tuberculin skin test using purified protein derivative (PPD) or an interferon-gamma release assay.

claims.text: Repeated pneumonia, poor growth or foul-smelling stools: chest X-ray and sweat test for cystic fibrosis.
claims.quote: Children with repeated episodes of pneumonia, poor growth, or foul-smelling stools should have a chest radiograph and sweat testing for cystic fibrosis.

claims.text: Acute cough with cold symptoms and no red flags is usually viral, and testing is rarely needed.
claims.quote: Acute cough in children with upper respiratory infection symptoms and no red flag findings is usually caused by a viral infection. Testing is rarely indicated unless it is necessary for infection control

claims.text: Bronchiolitis: RSV testing can be kept for children sick enough to be hospitalized.
claims.quote: Testing for RSV may be reserved for patients with illness severe enough to require hospitalization because it may guide isolation and bed assignment decisions.
